title: DFS in Reykjavík: Find the Route, Not the Shortcut!
description: Watch DFS explore Reykjavík (Miðborg) street-like nodes step-by-step, diving deep before it backtracks. You’ll see how depth-first search behaves on real-world style graphs—fast to traverse, but not always the shortest path.
ig_caption:
🗺️⚡ DFS in Reykjavík (Miðborg) is like choosing to “go all-in” down one street at a time. 

In graph theory terms, Depth-First Search (DFS) uses a stack (explicit or recursive) to traverse vertices by going as deep as possible before backtracking. On a mapped graph derived from real street intersections (nodes) and road segments (edges), DFS marks visited nodes to avoid cycles and guarantees it will reach a reachable target—though it may not return the shortest path.

🔬 What you’re seeing: 
✅ A path found through deep exploration + backtracking 
✅ Visited-state pruning to prevent infinite loops 
✅ The difference between “reachable” vs “optimal” routes

fb_caption:
Reykjavík street maps turned into a graph—then DFS goes exploring. 🌍➡️ DFS (Depth-First Search) is a classic graph search that dives deep along edges, uses a visited set to prevent cycles, and backtracks when it hits dead ends.
